questions.question: Explain why plastic waste is a problem in South Africa, giving figures and the environmental and economic costs.
questions.expected_answer: Plastics do not decay, so discarded items last for centuries, fragmenting into microplastics. South Africa generates about 2.4 million tonnes of plastic waste a year and recycles roughly 14 per cent; the rest goes to landfill, where space is running out, or escapes into the environment, blocking stormwater drains, choking rivers such as the Jukskei, polluting beaches and killing animals that eat or tangle in it. The costs include municipal drain and dump clearing, worse flooding when drains block, losses to fishing and tourism, dead livestock, and the wasted oil and gas from which the plastic was made, which is why measures such as the plastic bag levy and extended producer responsibility exist.

questions.question: Describe the three Rs, explain why they are arranged in that order, and give local examples of reduce and reuse.
questions.expected_answer: Reduce means using less plastic: shoppers using cloth bags, refillable bottles and loose vegetables, and manufacturers making thinner bottles, dropping unnecessary packaging and selling concentrates; the bag levy is a reduce measure. Reuse means using the same item again without reprocessing: a two-litre bottle as a water bottle, drip irrigator or eco-brick, a bucket as a planter, returnable crates and bottles, a lunchbox instead of bags. Recycle means collecting, sorting, washing, shredding and remelting thermoplastics into pellets for new products. The order is a cost ranking: reduce avoids waste entirely, reuse recovers almost all the value without processing, and recycling costs energy, collection, sorting and washing and recovers only part of the value with a loss of quality each time, so it comes last.

questions.question: Describe how plastic recycling works in South Africa, which plastics are economically recycled, and the limits of recycling.
questions.expected_answer: Used plastic is collected mainly by sixty to ninety thousand informal waste pickers, who sort it and sell it by the kilogram to buy-back centres, which bale it for recyclers; municipal separation-at-source and school collections are the organised side. Only thermoplastics can be remelted, and in practice PET bottles, HDPE bottles and drums, polypropylene crates and clean LDPE film pay, becoming fibre, pipes, bins, crates and refuse bags; polystyrene, multi-layer wrappers and dirty mixed film are uneconomic and go to landfill. Limits: contamination by food or the wrong plastic spoils a batch, sorting and washing cost money and water, and each remelt shortens the polymer chains so the recycled material usually serves a less demanding product, which is why recycling sits last in the hierarchy.
